slides.title: 15.1.2 Understanding Object Lifetime on the Heap
keyPoints: A new-expression ordinarily obtains storage and constructs an object in it.
The object’s lifetime continues until it is destroyed, commonly by a matching delete-expression or by an owning.
Losing the final owning access path does not cause raw dynamic storage to be reclaimed automatically.
Allocation can fail, and construction can fail after storage is obtained.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use 15.1.2 Understanding Object Lifetime on the Heap as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A new-expression ordinarily obtains storage and constructs an object in it. The object’s lifetime continues until it is destroyed, commonly by a matching delete-expression or by an owning abstraction. Losing the final owning access path does not cause raw dynamic storage to be reclaimed automatically. Allocation can fail, and construction can fail after storage is obtained. Standard new-expression rules handle certain construction-failure cleanup, but a sequence of several manually acquired resources can still leak if a later operation fails. Associate each successfully acquired resource with an owner immediately. Book II’s RAII design makes that rule systematic rather than dependent on every future return path. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use 15.2.1 Allocating Objects with new as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. new int{7} creates one dynamically allocated integer initialized to 7 and returns a pointer to it. new int[count]{} creates an array of value-initialized integers when the count is valid and the allocation succeeds. Validate sizes before converting external values to allocation counts; a negative signed input converted to a large unsigned value is not a sensible request. Ordinary throwing new reports allocation failure with an exception. Do not assume it returns null in that form. Nothrow allocation has a different interface and still requires a failure policy. For most application code, a vector or smart pointer expresses the ownership requirement more clearly and composes better with exceptions. slides.title: 15.2.2 Releasing Objects with delete
keyPoints: Use delete pointer for a matching single-object new-expression and delete[] pointer for a matching array.
Mixing those forms is invalid.
Deleting a null pointer is permitted, but deleting the same allocation twice or deleting storage not obtained.
Use delete pointer for a matching single-object new-expression and delete[] pointer for a matching array.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use 15.2.2 Releasing Objects with delete as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Use delete pointer for a matching single-object new-expression and delete[] pointer for a matching array new-expression. Mixing those forms is invalid. Deleting a null pointer is permitted, but deleting the same allocation twice or deleting storage not obtained through the matching mechanism is not. After deletion, pointers that referred to the destroyed object become dangling. Assigning null to one pointer can make that particular variable’s state clearer, but it does not update other aliases. Therefore pointer = nullptr is not a complete defense against use-after-free. A single, explicit owner and bounded borrowing relationships are the more reliable design. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.title: 15.3.1 Preventing Memory Leaks
keyPoints: A leak occurs when allocated resources remain unreleased and the program no longer has an appropriate way to.
Overwriting an owning raw pointer before deleting its allocation is one simple cause.
Returning early or throwing between allocation and cleanup is another.
A leak occurs when allocated resources remain unreleased and the program no longer has an appropriate way to.
slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use 15.3.1 Preventing Memory Leaks as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. A leak occurs when allocated resources remain unreleased and the program no longer has an appropriate way to reclaim them. Overwriting an owning raw pointer before deleting its allocation is one simple cause. Returning early or throwing between allocation and cleanup is another. Review every path, including failure paths, but recognize the limits of manual review. A resource-owning object whose destructor performs cleanup makes new return paths safer by construction. Leak detectors can identify some allocations left behind in executed tests, yet untested paths can still leak. Prefer designs where ownership is represented in a type rather than in a comment that each maintainer must remember. The graduate-level move is to ask what evidence would make the claim trustworthy: a compiler diagnostic, a runtime value, a preserved invariant, or a boundary that failed cleanly. slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use Trace ownership separately from arithmetic as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. In the manual function, values is the local owning pointer for this teaching allocation. The sum is copied into a local integer before release. After delete[], the function no longer accesses the array. Setting the pointer to null documents its local empty state, and returning the integer does not expose the expired storage. In the vector function, the local vector owns its sequence. The loop computes the same total. When the function exits, the vector’s lifetime ends and its resources are released through the library’s ownership behavior. No caller receives or deletes its internal data pointer. keyPoints: Why does a raw pointer’s destruction not release its target?

slides.narration: In this part of Chapter 15, use Review and solution reasoning as an engineering claim, not a vocabulary word. Why does a raw pointer’s destruction not release its target? The pointer is an address-holding object, not an automatic ownership policy. Release responsibility must be supplied by the program’s design. Why is a vector local not simply “all on the stack”? The owner object can have automatic lifetime while managing dynamic element storage. Owner location and owned storage are distinct. Why can two raw pointers cause double deletion? Copying an address does not create independent ownership. If both are treated as owners of one allocation, their release paths conflict.
